findings.paper_title: Mid Devon DC Auditor's Annual Report 2025-26 Draft for Audit Committee
findings.headline: Three categories of governance recommendations remain unimplemented after 2–3 years of audit recommendations
findings.detail: Repeated recommendations: (1) Risk mapping to corporate objectives recommended since 2023/24; partial progress (9 of 15 risks mapped as of Feb 2026). (2) Central gifts and hospitality register recommended since 2023/24; council promised Jan 2026 publication but not delivered; using physical log. (3) Compliance assurance mechanism (periodic member/officer declarations) recommended since 2022/23; no progress.
findings.matters: Persistent failure to implement governance recommendations across multiple audit cycles suggests weak implementation discipline or low prioritisation of soft controls.
findings.figures: Not specified
findings.quote: The Council does not include its corporate objectives or key performance indicators alongside the reporting of risks.

findings.paper_title: Mid Devon DC Auditor's Annual Report 2025-26 Draft for Audit Committee
findings.headline: Housing Revenue Account deficit of £852k driven by voids from regulatory compliance works
findings.detail: HRA reported £852k deficit in 2025/26. Key drivers: high void levels required by updated Decent Homes Standard and Awaab's Law implementation caused lost rental income while properties underwent remedial works and incurred higher reinstatement costs. Deficit was offset by transfer from HRA Housing Maintenance Earmarked Reserve.
findings.matters: Shows operational pressure on housing service from regulatory compliance costs. While managed through reserves this year, signals ongoing structural pressure affecting HRA sustainability.
findings.figures: £852k deficit
findings.quote: The Housing Revenue Account reported a deficit outturn £852k. Key drivers of the overspend were high levels of voids due to works to needed to comply with changes to the Decent Homes Standard and the introduction of Awaab's Law.

findings.paper_title: Mid Devon DC Auditor's Annual Report 2025-26 Draft for Audit Committee
findings.headline: Unresolved social rent calculation liability remains outstanding with DWP
findings.detail: Historic issue: council failed to set tenant rents to formula requirements for many years. Made refund payments of £780k in 2025/26 to non-welfare tenants. Provision reduced from £1.8m (2024/25) to £921k (2025/26). Council remains in discussions with DWP over settlement for welfare-recipient tenants, leaving final liability uncertain.
findings.matters: Represents both a control failure (wrong rents charged for years undetected) and an unquantified contingent liability dependent on DWP settlement.
findings.figures: £921k provision remaining; £780k refunds paid in 2025/26; prior provisions £1.8m (2024/25), £1.5m (2023/24)
findings.quote: The Council remains in discussions with the DWP over the rectification of this issue for tenants in receipt of housing benefit and Universal Credit.

findings.paper_title: Mid Devon DC Auditor's Annual Report 2025-26 Draft for Audit Committee
findings.headline: General Fund projected three-year deficit fell from £13.3m to £4.5m between September 2025 and February 2026 with no explanation
findings.detail: September 2025 MTFP identified cumulative deficits of £3.35m (2026/27), £4.7m (2027/28) and £5.79m (2028/29) totalling £13.3m. February 2026 update achieved a balanced 2026/27 and reset projections to £1.2m (2027/28), £1.3m (2028/29) and £2m (2029/30) totalling £4.5m. The £8.8m reduction is not explained in the report.
findings.matters: A two-thirds reduction in projected deficits signals either substantial unplanned savings or unrealistic budget assumptions. A lender must understand which.
findings.figures: Sept 2025: £3.35m, £4.7m, £5.79m (£13.3m cumulative); Feb 2026: £1.2m, £1.3m, £2m (£4.5m cumulative)
findings.quote: The General Fund MTFP identified deficits of £3.35m for 2026/27, £4.7m for 2027/28 and £5.79m in 2028/29. The cumulative budget gap over the three years is £13.3m.

findings.paper_title: Mid Devon DC Auditor's Annual Report 2025-26 Draft for Audit Committee
findings.headline: Housing Revenue Account contained material accounting error reversing income and expenditure classification
findings.detail: The HRA Income and Expenditure Account was materially misstated, showing net income when it should have shown net expenditure. This was identified during audit procedures and corrected.
findings.matters: Material errors in housing accounts represent control gaps in a major council service and indicate weak preventative controls.
findings.figures: Material error amount not disclosed
findings.quote: The Housing Revenue Account (HRA) Income and Expenditure Account contained a material error that led to the Account showing a net income on HRA Services for the year when it should have been net expenditure.

findings.paper_title: Mid Devon DC Auditor's Annual Report 2025-26 Draft for Audit Committee
findings.headline: Audit objection to financial statements prevents auditor from closing the audit
findings.detail: An objection to the 2025/26 financial statements has been received and is under consideration. The external auditor cannot issue the audit certificate until this objection is resolved, alongside completion of Whole of Government Accounts procedures.
findings.matters: Unresolved objections at draft stage are unusual and suggest potential credibility concerns with reported financial position.
findings.figures: Not specified
findings.quote: We have received an objection to the financial statements, which is currently being considered.

findings.paper_title: Audit Committee - final accounts 2025_26 covering report Sept 2026
findings.headline: The council claims strong reserves and financial position, though specific figures are not detailed in this covering report
findings.detail: The paper states that 'As can be seen from the reserve balances held, the Council remains in a strong position to deal with the funding challenges it faces' and operates with 'a strong culture of financial awareness'. However, actual reserve balances and control details are contained in the full Statement of Accounts, not in this covering report.
findings.matters: Reserve strength indicates capacity to absorb financial pressures and is material to lenders' assessment of financial resilience, though this claim would require verification from the full accounts
findings.figures: none in this report
findings.quote: As can be seen from the reserve balances held, the Council remains in a strong position to deal with the funding challenges it faces.

findings.paper_title: Audit Committee - final accounts 2025_26 covering report Sept 2026
findings.headline: A material error in the Housing Revenue Account was identified and corrected before final approval
findings.detail: An Excel formula error caused the HRA Income & Expenditure Account to incorrectly record (£192k) instead of £4,706k, overstating the surplus. The council identified and corrected the error before presenting final accounts to the audit committee, but the incident indicates control weaknesses in the accounts preparation process.
findings.matters: Material errors in accounts, even when corrected before approval, demonstrate control weaknesses in financial processes that are material to lenders' assessment of financial governance
findings.figures: (£192k) instead of £4,706k
findings.quote: There is one material change to note, where a figure of (£192k) was included within the Housing Revenue Account's Income & Expenditure Account (Section 15 page 117) instead of £4,706k, following an issue with Microsoft Excel leading to a formula not pulling through a figure. This therefore overstated the surplus.

findings.paper_title: Audit Committee - final accounts 2025_26 covering report Sept 2026
findings.headline: A member of the public has lodged a formal objection to the 2025/26 accounts
findings.detail: The paper states that 'there has been a formal objection to the accounts by a member of the public through the Public Inspection period' and that the external auditor Bishop Fleming is considering the objection and will provide a progress update to the committee. Formal public objections to council accounts are rare and typically signal concerns about accounting practices or financial reporting.
findings.matters: Formal objections to council accounts are unusual and may indicate audit findings or accounting issues that lenders and finance directors need to understand
findings.figures: none provided
findings.quote: The committee should note that there has been a formal objection to the accounts by a member of the public through the Public Inspection period. Bishop Fleming is considering the objection and will provide a progress update at the meeting.

findings.headline: Culm Garden Village capacity funding uncertain for next financial year after current funding secured
findings.detail: Government Homes England funding for Culm project team activities secured for current year but council has received no assurance of continued funding beyond 2026. Officers actively engaging with Homes England to seek renewal.
findings.matters: Discontinuance of funding would cause project team resourcing gap and risk of slippage on strategic housing development site affecting wider Devon housing supply.
findings.figures: Funding gap opens in next financial year; current funding confirmed only through 2025/26
findings.quote: Capacity funding was secured for the last financial year; however we do not currently have any assurances of funding for the next financial year.

findings.headline: Cyber security supply chain controls completed; overall cyber risk remains high severity with risk of ICO penalties and service denial
findings.detail: Supply chain risk management framework now complete (August 2026) with formal sign-off process through ICT/IM teams. Third-party risks monitored regularly through ITIG board. However, overall cyber security risk maintained at high severity (5) and likelihood (4) due to potential for data breaches, service denial, and ICO enforcement action.
findings.matters: Data breach could result in ICO fines, legal action, and service disruption. Supply chain controls critical as council increasingly depends on third-party suppliers.
findings.figures: Risk rating 20 (Severity 5, Likelihood 4)
findings.quote: CR2.7 marked as complete in August 2026.

findings.headline: Housing Rent Error now resolved: Regulator for Social Housing satisfied with council's corrective actions; recovery plan in place
findings.detail: Historic housing rent error has been formally resolved. Regulator for Social Housing published decision confirming satisfaction with actions taken. Regular monitoring arrangements established with RSH. Refund process progressing well for all cases except DWP Universal Credit cases which face DWP processing delays.
findings.matters: Serious reputational and regulatory issue now closed with regulator confidence. Demonstrates council's ability to manage crisis effectively and maintain regulatory standing.
findings.figures: Regulator engagement ongoing with regular monitoring
findings.quote: Regulatory decision published by Regulator of Social Housing (RSH) who are satisfied with actions taken to address historic error.

findings.headline: Housing supply accelerating: 75 new homes added 2025/26; temporary accommodation expansion funded and on track
findings.detail: Council added 75 homes to stock in 2025/26 with further completions at Willand and Bampton through HRA development programme. Temporary accommodation expansion underway: former vets property conversion commenced May 2026 on track; Ministry of Housing fund (Round 4) awarded supporting four additional TA properties.
findings.matters: Council is meeting statutory housing and homelessness prevention duties despite rising demand. TA expansion reduces future budget pressure from dispersed provision costs.
findings.figures: 75 new additions 2025/26; four additional TA properties funded
findings.quote: 75 new additions to stock 2025/26 and several more schemes in pipeline/live inc. recent completions at Willand and Bampton under Housing Revenue Account (HRA) development programme.

findings.headline: Cullompton Relief Road capital project on track: works commenced on site, all land secured, completion targeted early 2028
findings.detail: Major infrastructure project now in delivery phase with works commenced on site. All land assembled through compulsory purchase orders and land agreements. Sports club relocations progressing. Majority of works tendered. Project maintains healthy risk allowance with risks being managed and closed as work progresses.
findings.matters: Demonstrates council's ability to execute major capital infrastructure projects and maintain control through the transition period. Material capital commitment through to 2028 vesting date.
findings.figures: Completion early 2028; land assembly complete
findings.quote: Works to the Relief Road have now commenced on site and due for completion in early 2028. All land has been secured either via the confirmed compulsory purchase order or land agreements.

findings.headline: All Devon councils cease to exist April 1 2028; new councils created with Section 24 spending constraints to follow
findings.detail: Government decision made July 16 2026. All 11 current Devon councils end April 1 2028 and are replaced by four new unitary councils. Current councils' decisions cannot bind future councils. Section 24 spending directive constraints will be introduced ahead of vesting date.
findings.matters: Creates fundamental uncertainty about which entity holds responsibility for current council's borrowing obligations and commitments. Current council may commit to expenditure that successor council may reject or restructure.
findings.figures: Vesting date April 1 2028; four new councils created
findings.quote: The Government made its decision on the new form of local government for Devon on 16th July 2026. This will mean that all 11 councils in Devon cease to exist from 1st April 2028, with 4 brand new councils being created.

findings.headline: Medium-term financial planning severely constrained; budget gap closure efforts ongoing but described as extremely challenging after a decade of austerity
findings.detail: The council faces ongoing budget reductions whilst service costs rise due to inflationary pressures. LGR uncertainty through April 2028 prevents meaningful medium-term planning beyond 2027/28. Officers continue working to identify efficiencies and close the budget gap, but achieving this is described as extremely challenging.
findings.matters: Council's ability to service debt obligations and maintain service delivery through the restructuring period depends on resolving the underlying budget position.
findings.figures: None provided in document; over a decade of budget reductions implied
findings.quote: A range of options are being considered but over a decade of austerity make the situation extremely challenging.

findings.headline: Procurement strategy update is being deprioritized for Local Government Reorganisation compliance
findings.detail: A medium-priority recommendation for a procurement action plan (overdue since 31/07/2026) is being recommended for closure. The council has deprioritized this work in favour of embedding existing procurement strategy elements and ensuring compliance with Local Government Reorganisation by 1 April 2028. The existing 5-year strategy has less than 2 years remaining.
findings.matters: Shows the council is reorienting priorities toward a significant structural change, which may affect other medium-term strategic planning
findings.figures: 1 medium-priority recommendation overdue since 31/07/2026; LGR compliance deadline 1 April 2028
findings.quote: with focus shifting to LGR and being compliant from 1st April 2028 it is not deemed a priority to undertake this work.

findings.headline: Staff resignations in Property Services have delayed audit recommendations on asset management
findings.detail: Two medium-priority recommendations on corporate repairs and maintenance and void business property lease reviews have been delayed following resignations of key staff in Property Services. Both passed their 24/08/2026 target dates. A new Operations Manager has reviewed the backlog and is working through the items, but delivery remains slipped.
findings.matters: Staffing gaps affect ability to deliver control improvements and create continuity risk in asset and lease management
findings.figures: 2 medium-priority recommendations overdue since 24/08/2026; both in Property Services
findings.quote: Following the resignation of key staff in Property Services, this process has slipped.

findings.headline: High-priority patch management procurement policy recommendation is overdue and awaiting legal consultation
findings.detail: A high-priority recommendation to establish a procurement policy ensuring patch management availability from suppliers has passed its 31/08/2026 target date. The policy and supplier contract terms remain with Legal and Procurement for consultation and creation. Patch management is a fundamental IT control, and the delay suggests this control has not yet been properly embedded.
findings.matters: An overdue high-priority audit recommendation indicates an unresolved control weakness in IT security and procurement controls
findings.figures: 1 high-priority recommendation overdue since 31/08/2026
findings.quote: Policy and supplier standards still with Legal and Procurement for consultation and creation of specific contract terms and conditions.

findings.headline: Historic housing rent calculation error correction ongoing; £303k refunded in 2025/26.
findings.detail: Historic Social Rent calculation error from prior years. In 2025/26, council made 274 refunds totalling £303k net. Council has completed all corrections within its direct control; discussions continue with DWP and Regulator for Social Housing on remaining variances.
findings.matters: Shows prior control failure in financial governance over housing; ongoing correction demonstrates management attention but indicates governance control issue.
findings.figures: 274 refunds made, £303k net value (net of amounts owed and inclusive of compensation)
findings.quote: During the year, 274 refunds were made with the total net value of £303k. Work continues to address the error. All adjustments within the council's direct control have now been made, and discussions continue with the Department for Work & Pensions (DWP) in conjunction with the Regulator for Social Housing (RSH) about how to finalise the remaining variances.

findings.headline: Financial Sustainability is rated as the council's joint-highest corporate risk (20/25).
findings.detail: The corporate risk register rates Financial Sustainability (CR7) at 20 out of 25 maximum, joint-highest with Cyber Security and Local Government Reorganisation. Target is 12, indicating the council expects this to remain elevated.
findings.matters: High-rated financial sustainability risk signals budget pressures or long-term financial challenges that would concern lenders.
findings.figures: CR7 Financial Sustainability: current rating 20, target 12
findings.quote: CR7 Financial Sustainability Head of Finance, Property & Climate Resilience 20 12

findings.headline: Ten audit recommendations remain overdue.
findings.detail: At year-end, 57 audit recommendations were outstanding. Of these, 10 have passed their target date: 2 high priority, 5 medium priority, 3 low. This indicates management is not implementing agreed control improvements on schedule.
findings.matters: Shows management is not addressing audit-identified control weaknesses within agreed timescales, indicating weak governance execution.
findings.figures: 57 total recommendations outstanding, 10 overdue (2 high, 5 medium, 3 low)
findings.quote: In terms of overdue audit recommendations, there are currently two high priority, five medium priority, and three low priority actions or opportunities that are overdue.

findings.headline: Patch Management audit received Limited Assurance with three high-impact control failures.
findings.detail: Of audits completed by Devon Audit Partnership, one received Limited Assurance. Patch Management received Limited Assurance due to three high-impact observations. All three high-priority audit recommendations stem from this audit.
findings.matters: Indicates IT security or systems control failure; cybersecurity is separately rated as joint-highest corporate risk (20/25).
findings.figures: 1 Limited Assurance opinion, 3 high-impact observations, 3 high-priority recommendations
findings.quote: There was one "Limited Assurance" opinion on the Patch Management audit. Limited assurance has been provided due to the three high impact observations made within the report.

findings.headline: Prior Value for Money audit weaknesses have been remediated.
findings.detail: Bishop Fleming's 2024/25 audit included a Value for Money conclusion recognising good progress remediating significant weaknesses identified in prior year. The council has addressed these governance concerns.
findings.matters: Shows management has taken action to remediate prior audit concerns, improving governance and financial stewardship.
findings.figures: 2024/25 audit completed December 2025
findings.quote: The same Audit Committee considered the 2024/25 Value for Money opinion, recognising good progress has been made in remediating the significant weaknesses from previous year.

findings.paper_title: MDDC DAP Internal Audit Progress Report September 2026 - Final
findings.headline: Mandatory training arrangements lack formal policy and show compliance gaps across services
findings.detail: The audit found no formal Mandatory Training Policy despite training requirements being mandated. Training requirements are inconsistently defined and applied across services; testing identified compliance gaps; non-network users' training records are not consistently captured; and limited evidence exists of follow-up for overdue training. The audit provides Reasonable Assurance overall but identifies need for standardization and enhanced monitoring.
findings.matters: Compliance gaps in mandatory training could expose the council to regulatory or legal risk and may reflect wider control environment weaknesses affecting service delivery
findings.figures: Testing showed gaps in compliance, though the majority of sampled staff had been appropriately assigned mandatory training
findings.quote: in the absence of a formal Mandatory Training Policy, there is a risk that training requirements are inconsistently defined and applied, potentially leading to gaps in compliance and unclear accountability

findings.paper_title: MDDC DAP Internal Audit Progress Report September 2026 - Final
findings.headline: Service Charges audit finds limited assurance due to lapsed monitoring and documented undercharging of leaseholders
findings.detail: The Service Charges audit (draft status) identified lapsed monitoring of outstanding maintenance fees for extended periods, inconsistent recharging of maintenance costs with instances of undercharging resulting in financial loss to the Council, and control framework dependency on complex spreadsheet processes. The audit recommends formal review of the Leaseholder Policy and robust verification of recharges against actual spend. Critically, the full financial impact of undercharging could not be quantified.
findings.matters: A lender would be concerned about documented control weaknesses resulting in lost council income through undercharging, particularly given the inability to establish the full extent of losses
findings.figures: Full financial impact of undercharging unable to be quantified; audit remains at draft stage
findings.quote: Discussions with the Neighbourhood Team Leader (Income and Allocations) revealed that routine monitoring for outstanding maintenance fees had lapsed, with some accounts not reviewed for extended periods

findings.headline: Two audit actions being closed without completion due to Local Government Reorganisation resource pressures
findings.detail: A medium-priority procurement audit action plan and a low-priority staff appraisals action are both being closed without completion. The procurement action was delayed due to restructure, new PA23 regulations, and Finance vacancies; the council now deprioritizes it due to Local Government Reorganisation from 1 April 2028. The appraisals action is being closed because management time is consumed by LGR preparations. The council claims underlying objectives are being met through alternative means.
findings.matters: A lender would note that the council is deferring audit remediation work due to competing organisational demands, signalling resource constraints and trade-off decisions being driven by the forthcoming restructure.
findings.figures: Local Government Reorganisation scheduled for 1 April 2028; less than 2 years remaining on existing 5-year procurement strategy
findings.quote: There is less than 2 years left on the existing 5-year strategy, and with focus shifting to LGR and being compliant from 1st April 2028 it is not deemed a priority to undertake this work.

findings.headline: One high-priority audit recommendation is overdue
findings.detail: The council manages 41 audit actions: one high priority, 22 medium, and 18 low or opportunity. Nine actions are overdue, including one high-priority action. High-priority actions require Audit Committee agreement to extend deadlines. The specific nature of the overdue high-priority action is not disclosed in this summary.
findings.matters: A lender cares whether material control weaknesses are being remediated promptly; an overdue high-priority audit action indicates delayed or deferred remediation of a control weakness.
findings.figures: 1 of 41 audit actions is high-priority and overdue; 9 of 41 total are overdue
findings.quote: In terms of overdue audit recommendations, there is currently one high priority, three medium priority, and five low priority/ opportunity recommendations that are overdue (see Appendix 1).

findings.paper_title: Mid Devon District Council Audit Completion Report 2025-26 - Version to Audit Committee
findings.headline: Defined benefit pension gross surplus deteriorated by £1m while reported net liability improved marginally to £9.2m
findings.detail: The Council's gross defined benefit pension surplus on the LGPS decreased from £6.1m to £5.1m. However, under IFRIC 14 asset ceiling guidance the surplus is not recognised; instead a net pension liability of £9.2m is reported (2024/25: £9.6m), a £400k improvement. The discount rate used by the actuary increased from 5.80% to 6.10%. The reported improvement masks deterioration in the underlying funded position and is primarily driven by technical accounting adjustments.
findings.matters: Pension liabilities are material long-term financial obligations for councils; deterioration in the funded position indicates increased future contribution requirements, though the quantum of reported liability has marginally improved.
findings.figures: £6.1m to £5.1m (gross deficit movement), £9.6m to £9.2m (reported net liability), 5.80% to 6.10% (discount rate), £9.2m net liability (6.7x materiality threshold)
findings.quote: a net liability recognised of £9.2m (2024/25: £9.6m)

findings.paper_title: Mid Devon District Council Audit Completion Report 2025-26 - Version to Audit Committee
findings.headline: Property asset data held by Council continues not to reconcile with data used by external valuer; audit work in progress
findings.detail: Auditors' testing identified that Council records for some assets, including gross internal area for leisure centres, do not match data used by the District Valuer. This issue was flagged in the prior year audit and remains unresolved. Audit work on property valuations is still in progress. Council holds £47.5m of land and building assets and £163.7m of council dwellings, total £211m, on its balance sheet.
findings.matters: Property assets represent £211m of the Council's balance sheet; if supporting data is not properly reconciled to valuations, assets could be materially misstated and audit procedures may not detect the error.
findings.figures: £47.5m (land and buildings NBV at 31 March 2026), £163.7m (council dwellings NBV at 31 March 2026)
findings.quote: Our testing of PPE valuations identified that data held by the Council for some of its assets, such as the current gross internal area (GIA) of the leisure centres, did not agree with the data being used by the external valuer (District Valuer).

findings.paper_title: Mid Devon District Council Audit Completion Report 2025-26 - Version to Audit Committee
findings.headline: Valid objection to financial statements received; audit not yet concluded and audit certificate cannot be issued until resolved
findings.detail: An objection to the 2025/26 financial statements has been received and formally accepted by the auditors as valid. Work to investigate and resolve the objection is in progress. Until this is concluded, the auditors cannot issue their audit certificate, which effectively prevents closure of the audit. The nature of the objection is not disclosed in this report.
findings.matters: A valid objection indicates someone believes the accounts contain a material misstatement; this creates uncertainty about financial statement reliability until investigated. The unresolved objection means final audit sign-off is not yet assured.
findings.figures: One objection accepted as valid
findings.quote: An objection to the 2025/26 financial statements has been received. The objection has been accepted as valid for consideration and work is in progress on this currently.

findings.paper_title: Mid Devon District Council Audit Completion Report 2025-26 - Version to Audit Committee
findings.headline: Material £4.9m error in HRA Income and Expenditure Account due to formula failure; internal quality review missed it
findings.detail: The HRA statement initially showed net income of (£192k) when it should have shown net expenditure of £4,705k. The error resulted from a formula in the Excel workbook failing to update correctly during final amendments to the draft accounts. The Council's internal quality review process failed to identify this material misstatement before publication. The error was corrected in the final accounts presented for audit.
findings.matters: A material error escaping the internal quality review process signals a breakdown in financial control that undermines confidence in the accuracy and reliability of the financial statements and the Council's ability to produce reliable reporting.
findings.figures: £4,705k (correct figure), (£192k) (published figure), £4,897k (adjusted amount), materiality threshold £1,367k
findings.quote: There was a material error in the Housing Revenue Account (HRA) Income and Expenditure Account that led to the Account showing a net income on HRA Services for the year when it should have been net expenditure.

findings.headline: 2027/28 balance assumes £600k benefit from revised business rates forecast that requires validation
findings.detail: The council's proposed closure of the 2027/28 budget gap depends on a £600k reduction based on switching to a local business rates forecast (capturing two years of growth at circa £300k per year). The council explicitly states this requires 'validation of the local forecast', indicating the assumption has not yet been confirmed.
findings.matters: Unvalidated income assumptions create risk that the stated balanced budget position may not materialise if business rates forecasts prove optimistic
findings.figures: £600k benefit assumed, based on circa £300k annual growth
findings.quote: On average, there is circa £300k of growth in Business Rates each year, therefore, subject to validation of the local forecast, an estimated £600k reduction in the projected shortfall may be achievable.

findings.headline: Service delivery reductions stated as likely without significant additional savings
findings.detail: The report explicitly warns that the scale of funding reductions means it is unlikely the council can fully balance the budget without significant service implications. Earlier sections note that staffing reductions through natural turnover will stretch service delivery and lead to lower provision levels.
findings.matters: Service reductions may impair statutory functions, operational resilience, or council effectiveness and signal financial stress
findings.figures: Not quantified; applies to 2027/28 onwards
findings.quote: Whilst every effort will be made to identify efficiency savings, given the scale of the likely funding reductions it is unlikely that a sufficient level can be identified to fully balance the 2027/28 budget without significant implications on service provision.

findings.headline: Housing Revenue Account faces £1.5m shortfall with development programme viability now under formal review
findings.detail: The HRA shortfall of £1,491k for 2027/28 is driven by regulatory cost pressures (Awaab's Law, Decent Homes Standard, Renters Rights) and rising financing costs for housing development. Mid Devon Housing is conducting a formal viability and sustainability review, specifically testing build specification (net zero vs EPC B), tenure mix, cost assumptions, borrowing levels, and grant funding.
findings.matters: Housing development programmes represent major borrowing commitments; formally reviewing viability signals potential retrenchment and programme delivery risk
findings.figures: £1,491k HRA shortfall 2027/28, rising to £5,923k by 2029/30
findings.quote: Currently Mid Devon Housing is reviewing their viability and sustainability, particularly in respect of the ambitious development programme.

findings.headline: General Fund Reserve margin is minimal at only £91k above the £2m minimum
findings.detail: As at 31 March 2026, the council holds £2,091k in General Fund Reserve against a £2m minimum. The council plans to draw £500k from reserves to help balance 2027/28, which would bring reserves to near-minimum levels, leaving virtually no financial cushion.
findings.matters: Minimal reserve buffer limits the council's ability to absorb unplanned costs or revenue shortfalls and indicates tight financial management
findings.figures: £2,091k held, £2m minimum threshold, £500k planned draw
findings.quote: As at 31 March 2026, the Council holds £2,091k in the General Fund Reserve, £91k above the recommended minimum

findings.headline: General Fund budget gap escalates from £1.6m (2027/28) to £5.5m (2029/30)
findings.detail: The council faces a £1,601k shortfall in 2027/28 which grows significantly to £5,486k by 2029/30. The council describes this as a cumulative figure without remedial action. The escalation is driven by Local Government Finance Settlement funding reductions combined with inflation and known service pressures.
findings.matters: An accelerating multi-year deficit indicates structural financial challenge rather than cyclical pressure, affecting medium-term lending risk and sustainability
findings.quote: For the General Fund, this estimated a funding shortfall for 2027/28 of £1,601k, and is due to rise significantly to £5,486k by 2029/30.

findings.headline: Planned maintenance deferred: £270,000 of budgeted work not yet started.
findings.detail: Significant planned maintenance work totalling £270,000 has not begun; the report states schedules are 'being scoped and will be tendered' with work 'yet to be started'.
findings.matters: Deferred maintenance accumulates into larger future capital costs and may indicate asset management constraints or cash pressure.
findings.figures: £270,000 unstarted
findings.quote: Planned Maintenance schedules being scoped and will be tendered - work has yet to be started (270,000)

findings.headline: Investment income down £60,000 due to reduced cash balances.
findings.detail: The council's interest receivable has fallen by £60,000 because cash balances have declined.
findings.matters: Falling cash balances and reduced investment returns signal tightening liquidity or reserve depletion.
findings.figures: £60,000 reduction
findings.quote: Investment income down due to reduced cash balances 60,000

findings.headline: Planning enforcement understaffed: £65,000 agency overspend due to permanent recruitment failure.
findings.detail: The planning enforcement team cannot fill permanent vacancies and is overspending £65,000 on agency staff to maintain service delivery.
findings.matters: Recruitment failure in statutory services signals labour market challenges or wage competitiveness issues that point to broader council staffing stress.
findings.figures: £65,000 agency overspend
findings.quote: Agency staff overspend in enforcement due to difficulty in recruitment of permanent staff 65,000

findings.headline: Temporary accommodation: £50,000 overspend as homelessness costs rise.
findings.detail: The homelessness and rough sleeping service is running £50,000 over budget on temporary accommodation, suggesting rising unit costs or increased case volumes—or both.
findings.matters: Rising homelessness and accommodation costs are indicators of deprivation, housing market strain, and growing demand on council budgets.
findings.figures: £50,000 overspend
findings.quote: Estimated overspend on temporary accommodation 50,000

findings.headline: Planning income falling sharply: statutory planning fees £200,000 below prior-year Q1.
findings.detail: The council's Q1 2026/27 planning fee income is running £200,000 behind the equivalent quarter in 2025/26. Concurrently, the planning enforcement team is overspending £65,000 on agency staff due to recruitment difficulty, and legal costs are running £30,000 over budget for appeals. This paints a picture of reduced development activity and understaffing in a key income-generating function.
findings.matters: Structural decline in planning income indicates softening economic activity and development; the council cannot offset this with savings in enforcement because it cannot recruit permanent staff.
findings.figures: £200,000 income shortfall; £65,000 enforcement agency overspend; £30,000 legal overspend
findings.quote: Q1 performance of statutory planning fees and charges down on last year Q1 200,000

findings.headline: Waste services crisis: £340,000 agency overspend from vacancies, sickness, and increased household collections.
findings.detail: Waste services is overspending significantly on agency staff to cover permanent staffing gaps and sickness absence while managing higher-than-budgeted collection volumes. This is compounded by fuel cost increases (£66,000), motor insurance rises (£36,400), and additional hired vehicles (£10,000). Salary savings of £160,000 are being overwhelmed by £340,000 in agency costs, netting a £180,000 overspend in this single service.
findings.matters: Reliance on expensive temporary staffing in an essential service signals persistent recruitment failure and structural cost escalation that will not reverse without action.
findings.figures: £340,000 agency overspend; £66,000 fuel; £36,400 insurance; £10,000 hired vehicles
findings.quote: Increased agency due to vacancies, sickness and increased household collections 340,000

findings.headline: General Fund reserve forecast to decline by £455,938 to £1,635,453
findings.detail: The General Fund reserve is forecast to fall from £2,091,391 (31 March 2026) to £1,635,453 (31 March 2027). This £455,938 draw represents the in-year deficit being absorbed into reserves.
findings.matters: Declining reserves reduce financial flexibility and headroom for unexpected costs or revenue shortfalls. Continued reserve depletion at this rate affects borrowing capacity and financial sustainability.
findings.quote: General Fund Reserve 31/03/26 (2,091,391) ... Forecast General Fund Balance 31/03/2027 (1,635,453)

findings.headline: Planning overspending by £361,400; council funding £180,900 from earmarked reserves
findings.detail: Planning is forecast to overspend by £361,400 (19.2% of budget). The council is offsetting this partly by drawing £180,900 from earmarked reserves, leaving a net variance of £180,500. This depletes reserves intended for specific planned purposes.
findings.matters: Using earmarked reserves to cover current service overspends erodes the council's ability to fund planned capital or specific initiatives and signals cash management pressures.
findings.figures: Budget £941,440, Forecast £1,302,840, Overspend £361,400, Transfer from EMR £180,900, Net variance £180,500

findings.headline: Homelessness & Rough Sleeping overspending by £50,000 (34.5% of budget)
findings.detail: Homelessness is forecast to spend £194,720 against a budget of £144,720, a 34.5% variance. This suggests unexpected demand for temporary accommodation or cost increases in the homelessness response.
findings.matters: Welfare-driven overspends are difficult to reverse mid-year and often persist. A 34% variance indicates the budget was materially misestimated or demand conditions have changed, both of which affect forecast reliability.
findings.figures: Budget £144,720, Forecast £194,720, Variance £50,000 (34.5%)
findings.quote: Homelessness & Rough Sleeping GF2d 144,720 18,143 194,720 50,000 0 50,000 34.5%

findings.headline: Waste Services forecasting £360,900 overspend (24.2% of budget)
findings.detail: Waste Services is the largest variance in the budget, with a full-year forecast of £1,854,360 against a budget of £1,493,460. This 24% overspend is material and suggests either sustained demand pressures, inflation in disposal costs, or operational cost control issues.
findings.matters: A quarter of a service's budget overrunning indicates systematic cost pressures, not one-off timing issues. If waste inflation or service demand is the driver, this will recur and constrain future budget flexibility.

findings.headline: Multiple car parks underperforming, including Market Car Park Tiverton (£7,117 Q1 shortfall)
findings.detail: Several council car parks are tracking below budget in Q1. Market Car Park Tiverton shows a £7,117 variance, Phoenix House Tiverton a £2,143 variance, and Westexe South Tiverton a £3,555 variance.
findings.matters: Car parking income is controllable and sensitive to demand; consistent underperformance across multiple sites may indicate broader demand problems or pricing misalignment
findings.figures: Market Car Park, Tiverton: Variance -£7,117; Phoenix House: Variance -£2,143; Westexe South: Variance -£3,555

findings.headline: Market income forecast to fall 22% short of budget
findings.detail: Market Income is forecast to underperform by £25,000 against an annual budget of £113,180, representing a -22% variance. This is the largest percentage shortfall among major income streams listed.
findings.matters: A 22% income shortfall in a specific controllable revenue stream suggests either unrealistic budget assumptions or a significant decline in market use
findings.figures: Annual Budget £113,180, Full Year Forecast Variation -£25,000 (-22%)

findings.headline: General Fund fees and charges forecast £245,000 shortfall across all income lines
findings.detail: Total General Fund fees and charges of £8,604,110 are forecast to underperform by £245,000 in the full year (-2.8%). The shortfall spans multiple income streams including planning, car parking, market income, and garden waste.
findings.matters: A council-wide 2.8% underperformance in fees and charges indicates whether the authority's income projections are realistic and affects overall budget sustainability
findings.figures: Total Annual Budget £8,604,110, Full Year Forecast Variation -£245,000 (-2.8%)

findings.headline: Planning Fees forecast £200,000 short of annual budget at -19%
findings.detail: The Planning Fees budget of £1,053,000 is forecast to underperform by £200,000 in the full year, a -19% variance. Planning income is a material income line for the council.
findings.matters: An income shortfall of this magnitude in a controllable fee stream signals either unrealistic budget assumptions or a decline in planning activity, both of which affect the council's financial flexibility
findings.figures: Annual Budget £1,053,000, Full Year Forecast Variation -£200,000 (-19%)

findings.headline: Total agency staffing costs are forecast £586,000 over budget, a 915% variance on a £64,020 annual budget
findings.detail: The council budgeted £64,020 for all agency staff but Q1 actual costs were £215,280 against a profiled budget of £16,005 (£199,275 over). The full year forecast shows total agency overspend of £586,000, more than nine times the original budget allocation.
findings.matters: Council-wide agency overspend of this scale signals structural staffing problems across multiple services that are consuming unexpected resources and eroding budget predictability.
findings.figures: Total annual agency budget £64,020; Q1 budget £16,005, Q1 actual £215,280; forecast overspend £586,000 (915.3% variance)

findings.headline: Waste Services is forecast to overspend agency costs by £340,000 on an annual budget of £42,860
findings.detail: Waste Services budgeted £42,860 for agency staffing but in Q1 spent £88,204—£77,489 over the quarterly budget of £10,715. The full year forecast shows a £340,000 overspend, a 793.3% variance. This is by far the largest agency cost overspend in the council.
findings.matters: Extreme agency reliance in a core service suggests the council cannot recruit or retain permanent waste staff, creating unplanned cost pressure and operational risk that affects service delivery and financial stability.
findings.figures: Annual budget £42,860; Q1 budget £10,715, Q1 actual £88,204; forecast overspend £340,000 (793.3% variance)

findings.headline: Capital programme slippage of £17.9m, primarily Cullompton relief road delays
findings.detail: Against revised deliverable capital budget of £51,654k, forecast spend only £34,173k, with £17,968k slippage. Major delays to Cullompton Town Centre Relief Road (construction now expected mid-August) plus setbacks in solar project tendering.
findings.matters: Significant capital slippage indicates project delivery risk, possible re-phasing of investment returns, and delays to economic regeneration benefits
findings.figures: £17,968k slippage; £5,430k from General Fund capital projects; relief road is material component
findings.quote: The forecast slippage is largely from the delays to the Cullompton Town Centre Relief Road, with construction works now expected to begin in mid-August. There are also setbacks in tendering the planned solar projects.

findings.headline: Governance failure: historic social rent calculation errors with 402 tenant refunds of £330k
findings.detail: Council identified and corrected long-standing errors in social rent calculations from 20 January 2025. 402 tenant refunds totalling £330,210 issued including £13,775 compensation. Complexity remains with benefit cases pending DWP confirmation. Regulator fully engaged.
findings.matters: Governance failures with tenant impact raise regulatory compliance risk; regulator involvement could signal broader financial control weaknesses
findings.figures: 402 refunds; £330,210 total; £13,775 compensation
findings.quote: To date, 402 refunds have been issued to tenants, with a total value of £330,210; this includes £13,775 in compensation.

findings.headline: Capital funding strategy shifted from PWLB borrowing to reserve drawdowns
findings.detail: Council announced shift to funding housing development via reserves rather than PWLB borrowing, eliminating the £1,016k annual PWLB smoothing contribution. This strategy is unsustainable long-term as reserves are finite and investment income has fallen £438k year-on-year.
findings.matters: Reserve depletion is not a sustainable long-term funding strategy; declining available borrowing headroom limits flexibility for emergency funding or opportunities
findings.figures: £1,016k PWLB contribution removed; investment income forecast £163k vs £601k outturn (£438k shortfall); cash balances reduced
findings.quote: Following the change in approach announced at 2025/26 Outturn to fund the ambitious housing development scheme by utilising reserves rather than borrowing funds, the annual budgeted contribution to the PWLB Smoothing Reserve is no longer required.

findings.headline: HRA facing £200k social rent income loss due to delayed new housing delivery
findings.detail: Planned social housing development is delayed, reducing predicted rent income by £200k. Simultaneously, sustained high void levels are creating £130k expenditure pressure from increased relets costs and legislative compliance requirements (Awaab's law, Decent Homes Standard).
findings.matters: HRA is capital-intensive; delays in delivery pipeline undermine financial projections and create cost pressures that could require subsidy from General Fund
findings.figures: £200k income shortfall; £130k void cost pressure
findings.quote: £200k Loss of predicted social rent income due to delays in new housing coming on-line... £130k Additional expenditure pressure on the high sustained levels of voids and the increased cost of bringing them back into occupation.

findings.headline: Agency staff costs exceeding salary savings by £173k, driven by recruitment failures
findings.detail: Despite £282k targeted vacancy savings, the council has been forced to use expensive agency staff to cover vacant positions, particularly in waste services due to vacancies, sickness and growth in housing collections. The cost of agency cover more than offsets the vacancy savings.
findings.matters: Persistent inability to recruit to permanent roles indicates operational and service delivery risk; agency costs are non-recoverable and reduce flexibility
findings.figures: £282k vacancy target savings; £173k net agency cost overspend; £413k net employee underspend after both factors
findings.quote: The cost of the agency staff more than offsets the corresponding General Fund services staffing underspends by £173k. The most significant is within waste services due to covering increased vacancies and sickness compared to previous years, plus additional collections required arising from the growth in housing.

findings.headline: Planning income £245k below budget reflecting subdued housing market
findings.detail: Planning fee income is running significantly below forecast due to weak housing market confidence and delayed major schemes. This reflects broader economic weakness in the authority's area and reduced development pipeline.
findings.matters: Planning income volatility and weakness indicates underlying economic stress in the local area; persistent shortfalls are difficult to recover and compress budgets
findings.figures: £245k income variance below budget; planning fee is primary component
findings.quote: the Planning income is once again well below the budgeted forecast, reflecting the subdued housing market. There have been delays in some major schemes expected to be submitted.

findings.headline: General Fund reserve forecast to fall below £2m minimum threshold to £1,636k
findings.detail: The projected overspend of £456k will reduce General Fund reserves below the council's agreed minimum balance of £2m. Section 2.4 states the council will review this position at year-end 'where we reflect on levels of reserves and the significant loss of central government core funding, plus any short-term implications of preparing for Local Government Reorganisation.'
findings.matters: General Fund reserve adequacy is a key credit metric for lenders; falling below minimum thresholds indicates financial stress and limited capacity to absorb unforeseen shocks
findings.figures: £1,636k forecast vs £2m minimum; £456k overspend; opening balance £2,091k
findings.quote: If the forecast level of overspend is delivered, this will indicatively increase the General Reserve balance to £1,686k, below the agreed minimum £2m balance.

findings.headline: Treasury adviser forecasts interest rates will increase to 4%–4.25% and inflation pressures will persist through 2027
findings.detail: The council's treasury adviser (MUFG Corporate Markets) expects Bank Rate to rise from 3.75% to 4%–4.25% 'over the coming months' and warns that Middle East conflict and energy cost pressures are likely to push UK inflation above 4% by late spring 2026, constraining rate cuts.
findings.matters: Rising rates will increase borrowing costs when the council must resume new borrowing, potentially squeezing capital spending or requiring service reductions. The forecast is material to the council's financial planning.
findings.figures: Bank Rate 3.75% (end March 2026). PWLB 5-year rate 5.28%, 10-year 5.72%. Forecast: Bank Rate 4.0–4.25% within months; CPI inflation forecast above 4.5%.
findings.quote: At the start of April 2026, the market expected Bank Rate to increase over the coming months to 4% or 4.25%, from 3.75%.

findings.headline: Council's internal borrowing strategy explicitly flagged as unsustainable if interest rates remain elevated
findings.detail: The council maintained an under-borrowed position (borrowing £31.4m against a capital financing requirement of £63.3m) by using cash reserves instead of taking new loans. The treasury report notes this policy 'has been kept under review to avoid incurring higher borrowing costs in the future when this Authority may not be able to avoid new borrowing.'
findings.matters: When reserves are exhausted or interest rates fall enough that borrowing becomes affordable again, the council will face borrowing costs that may be significantly higher than anticipated if rates have risen.
findings.figures: CFR £63.3m, gross borrowing £31.4m, under-funding position £35.9m funded by reserves.
findings.quote: The policy of avoiding new borrowing by running down spare cash balances, has served the Council well over the last few years. However, this has been kept under review to avoid incurring higher borrowing costs in the future when this Authority may not be able to avoid new borrowing to finance capital expenditure.

findings.headline: Investment income fell 16% short of budget due to lower cash balances and interest rate cuts
findings.detail: The council achieved £891k investment return against a budget of £1,062k. The shortfall is attributed to Bank Rate reductions totalling 0.75% during the year and the deliberate reduction in cash held for investment purposes.
findings.matters: Reduces income available to support services and demonstrates sensitivity to interest rate movements.
findings.figures: Actual return £891k vs budget £1,062k (£171k shortfall). Average internally managed balance £15.3m earning 3.94% vs SONIA benchmark 4.01%.
findings.quote: The Council made a total return of £891k from investments in 2025/26 against a budget of £1,062k.

findings.headline: Investment portfolio reduced by 68% to hoard cash for capital spending as part of internal borrowing strategy
findings.detail: All £10.5m of internally managed short-term investments matured during 2025/26 and were not reinvested. The council now holds only £5m in CCLA property funds. This is part of a deliberate strategy to use reserves to fund capital spending and avoid new borrowing at high rates.
findings.matters: Reduces council income from treasury investments and signals the council is using reserves as its primary funding source for capital, raising questions about sustainability when reserves deplete.
findings.figures: Treasury investments: £15,500k (31 Mar 2025) → £5,000k (31 Mar 2026). Internally managed funds: £10,500k → £0k.
findings.quote: Reducing cash balances has also meant a greater proportion of the Council's internally managed funds have been held in its NatWest call account, giving a lower average rate of return.

findings.headline: Cyber and information security risks recognized as material, with MHCLG grant awarded but significant investment still required
findings.detail: Cyber security (CR2) and information security (CR5) are flagged as high-risk governance issues. The council received 'a significant grant from MHCLG to support further investment in strengthening information security,' which implies the baseline position was insufficient. No specific cyber incident is reported, but the governance language suggests an existing capability gap.
findings.matters: Cyber attacks against councils can disrupt financial systems and compromise data. The fact MHCLG is funding remediation suggests the sector-wide concern is material, and this council needed external support.
findings.figures: CR2 (Cyber Security): rating 20, target 15; CR5 (Information Security): rating 12, target 8
findings.quote: Cyber and information security are recognised as significant governance risks. The Council has undertaken an independent assessment against the Cyber Assessment Framework, which has informed an Improvement Implementation Plan approved by management. The ITIG Board... and staff have worked closely with key technical and assurance partners resulting in a significant grant from MHCLG to support further investment in strengthening information security.

findings.headline: Local Government Reorganisation creates material governance uncertainty with risk of control degradation during transition
findings.detail: The council explicitly identifies local government reorganisation (CR19) as a top-tier governance risk (rating 20 of 25, target 15). The statement warns of 'reduced clarity of accountability and decision-making, pressure on senior officer and member capacity, potential weakening of internal controls and statutory oversight, loss of organisational knowledge, and short-term decision-making driven by uncertainty over future structures.' These describe a governance environment unstable enough to affect lending decisions.
findings.matters: Lenders need clarity on whether management and internal controls will remain effective during a reorganisation that could reshape the entity itself. The council is flagging that this period carries material governance risk.
findings.figures: Risk rating 20 (current), target 15
findings.quote: Future local government reorganisation creates governance risks for the Council during the transition period. These include reduced clarity of accountability and decision-making, pressure on senior officer and member capacity, potential weakening of internal controls and statutory oversight, loss of organisational knowledge, and short-term decision-making driven by uncertainty over future structures.

findings.headline: Patch Management audit returned Limited Assurance with three high-priority findings still unaddressed
findings.detail: Internal Audit found significant IT control weaknesses. As of year-end, three high-priority recommendations (all from Patch Management) remain open, plus two additional high-priority findings are overdue. This indicates either resource constraints or operational difficulty in implementing security controls. The policy states high-priority actions require Audit Committee agreement to extend timelines.
findings.matters: Unpatched systems are a material cyber risk and insurance concern. The fact that high-priority IT findings are overdue signals either weak control discipline or operational capacity issues.
findings.figures: 3 high-priority recommendations open; 2 high-priority recommendations overdue; 57 total recommendations tracked
findings.quote: There was one "Limited Assurance" opinion on the Patch Management audit. Limited assurance has been provided due to the three high impact observations made within the report. In terms of overdue audit recommendations, there are currently two high priority, five medium priority, and three low priority actions or opportunities that are overdue.

findings.headline: Social housing rent overpayment error remains partially unresolved with £303k refunded in 2025/26
findings.detail: The council has completed all adjustments within its direct control, but discussions continue with DWP and the Regulator for Social Housing on remaining variances. This represents an ongoing contingent liability where the final quantum is not yet settled. The council quantified it as requiring 274 refunds totalling £303k net of compensation during the year.
findings.matters: A lending decision requires understanding the full extent of this liability and whether further refunds are likely. The fact it remains unresolved after years suggests execution or regulatory complexity.
findings.figures: 274 refunds made, £303k total net value (inclusive of compensation)
findings.quote: During the year, 274 refunds were made with the total net value of £303k. Work continues to address the error. All adjustments within the council's direct control have now been made, and discussions continue with the Department for Work & Pensions (DWP) in conjunction with the Regulator for Social Housing (RSH) about how to finalise the remaining variances.

findings.headline: HRA development programme funding deferred by drawing £10.1m from earmarked reserves instead of external borrowing to avoid current interest rates
findings.detail: Rather than borrow externally for HRA housing development, the council chose to draw £10,145k from earmarked reserves (£7.8m from Premium Deficit for PWLB Loan Reserve, £2.3m from Housing Maintenance Fund, £63k from Renewable Energy Fund). This decision explicitly delays borrowing 'until interest rates are more favourable' and reduces the council's financial cushion.
findings.matters: Timing borrowing to avoid current rates shows confidence in future rate improvement but also increases refinancing risk if rates stay high or rise further; drawing reserves for routine capital reduces capacity for unexpected costs.
findings.figures: £10,145k drawn from HRA earmarked reserves for development programme; £7,794k from Premium Deficit for PWLB Loan Reserve
findings.quote: This delays the need for borrowing until interest rates are more favourable. Therefore, in addition to the £852k draw from the Housing Maintenance Fund to offset the in-year overspend, a further draw of £7,794k has been taken from the Premium Deficit for PWLB Loan Reserve

findings.headline: Agency staffing spend more than doubled to £948k despite meeting vacancy target; recruitment and retention challenges continue
findings.detail: Agency costs increased from £523k (2024/25) to £948k (2025/26), a 81% rise, even though the council exceeded its corporate vacancy target of £282k. Staffing absences were concentrated in Finance, Legal, Planning Enforcement, and Waste. Turnover was 15.46% (lower than prior years) but sickness increased 22% to 8.31 days per FTE.
findings.matters: High and rising agency spend signals either structural recruitment failure in key control functions (Finance, Legal) or capacity constraints that may affect service delivery and financial controls.
findings.figures: Agency costs: £523k (2024/25) to £948k (2025/26); vacancy target £282k; turnover 15.46%; sickness 8.31 days per FTE, up 22%
findings.quote: the Council continues to struggle with recruitment and retention. There were continued pockets of absence in key services, particularly Finance, Legal, Planning Enforcement and Waste requiring higher usage of agency staff than planned. Overall agency spend was £948k which was a marked increase on the £523k in 2024/25.

findings.headline: Historic housing rent calculation error identified and correction underway; regulator fully engaged
findings.detail: A calculation error in historic social rent charges was corrected effective 20 January 2025. As of 18 May 2026, 406 tenant refunds totalling £321,764 (including £11,775 in compensation) had been issued, with a further 10 cases pending. Cases where Universal Credit is involved await DWP guidance. The regulator has been kept informed with latest meeting on 28 May 2026.
findings.matters: An identified error in rent calculations, even if now corrected, indicates control weaknesses in the billing/revenue system and regulatory oversight suggests reputational or compliance risk.
findings.figures: 406 refunds issued totalling £321,764; £11,775 in compensation; 10 cases pending; UC cases awaiting DWP guidance
findings.quote: there was an underlying error identified within the historic calculation of Social Rents. The calculation was corrected, and independently verified, with correct charges raised since 20 January 2025. The process of identifying the corrections and processing refunds has been ongoing since that point. The regulator is also fully engaged and kept informed.

findings.headline: £18.3m capital slippage including HRA development delays: planning permission delays, no bids on tenders, unforeseen water/sewerage complications
findings.detail: Of a £42.4m capital programme, £18.3m slipped to future years, with £11m from HRA housing development alone. The slippage was driven by delays in obtaining planning permission, failed tender processes, contract signing delays, and discovery of unmapped water/sewerage infrastructure. HRA development projects also incurred £2.8m in unforeseen additional costs (alterations, demolition, S106 contributions, storage of completed units).
findings.matters: Significant capital slippage in a development programme signals project delivery risk and management capacity constraints; unforeseen infrastructure costs indicate inadequate pre-project investigation.
findings.figures: £18,320k slippage; £10,966k from HRA housing development; £2,830k overspends on HRA development
findings.quote: various projects within the HRA housing development programme driven mainly by delays in obtaining planning permission, no bids being received on tenders, delays in contract signing and the discovery of unforeseen complications such as uncharted water mains / sewerage pipes

findings.headline: Cash position has reached near-minimum operational level; external borrowing expected imminently for cash flow
findings.detail: Despite no external borrowing in 2025/26, internally managed funds fell from £21.2m to £15.3m because capital spending drew down cash balances. The council now explicitly states cash has 'almost reached the lowest operational point' and external borrowing is 'expected this calendar year mainly for cash flow purposes' — a shift from funding capital via internal resources to requiring external debt.
findings.matters: Moving from cash-backed capital spending to external borrowing at a time of uncertain interest rates signals tightening liquidity and reduced financial flexibility for other priorities or emergencies.
findings.figures: Internally managed funds: £21.2m (2024/25) to £15.3m (2025/26); interest earned: £1,037k to £891k
findings.quote: cash balances have almost reached the lowest operational point and therefore external borrowing is expected this calendar year mainly for cash flow purposes.

findings.headline: HRA overspend of £852k driven by void crisis: voids up 116%, void costs up 67%
findings.detail: The Housing Revenue Account overspent by £852k (6.41% of budget), primarily because exceptional vacancy levels following Awaab's Law compliance and Decent Homes Standard changes generated both higher void-related costs and lost rental income. Void numbers have nearly doubled year-on-year with associated contractor and material costs rising 67%. The overspend is being funded from the HRA Housing Maintenance Earmarked Reserve.
findings.matters: Void-driven losses signal that compliance with new regulations is creating structural cost pressures on the HRA, and the council is now drawing reserves to offset annual deficits rather than investing in new housing.
findings.figures: £852k HRA overspend; voids risen 116%; void costs increased 67%; Awaab's Law mentioned as driver
findings.quote: Voids have risen from the previous year by 116%. Void costs (contractors and materials) have also increased by 67%.

findings.paper_title: Mid Devon Council Tax Empty Homes & Second Homes Premiums Policy 2026
findings.headline: Council is implementing empty homes and second homes premiums as a revenue-raising measure due to acknowledged financial pressure.
findings.detail: Mid Devon is using new Council Tax premiums to raise income from empty dwellings (100% after 1 year, 200% after 5 years, 300% after 10 years) and second homes (100%). The council explicitly links this to financial pressure. Revenue goes into the Collection Fund and is shared with major precepting authorities. However, any discretionary reductions granted for hardship must be financed from the council's general fund, creating potential downside variance to expected income.
findings.matters: Lenders need to understand whether councils are relying on new revenue sources to manage budget gaps. This policy shows Mid Devon is pursuing new tax income, but without projections of how many properties will be affected or expected revenue, the materiality to the council's finances is unclear.
findings.figures: Empty homes: 100% premium (1+ years empty), 200% (5+ years), 300% (10+ years); Second homes: 100% premium
findings.quote: The continued pressure on local authority finances (both the Council and the Major Preceptors) together with the need to encourage all owners of domestic premises to bring them back into use, makes it essential that the Council changes its approach to empty homes.

findings.headline: Cash balances declining with investment income falling from £1.2m to £586k
findings.detail: The council reports cash balances have reduced during 2025/26 and will reduce further in 2026/27. Investment returns have fallen sharply from £1,191k in 2023/24 to £586k forecast for 2025/26 as interest rate cuts erode returns. The council is managing investment maturity profiles to match large cash outflows.
findings.matters: Declining reserves combined with falling investment income reduces the financial buffer to absorb variations in capital spending or unexpected revenue pressures
findings.figures: Investment returns: £1,191k (2023/24) → £1,037k (2024/25) → £586k (2025/26); cash balances declining
findings.quote: Cash balances have reduced during 2025/26, and will reduce further in 2026/27, so there will be a need to further reduce the average maturity on investments to ensure a regular turnover of maturities, which will be matched with the Council's large cash outflows.

findings.headline: General Fund financing costs also rising from 5.69% to 9.44% over three years
findings.detail: General Fund financing costs as a percentage of net revenue stream are forecast to rise from 5.69% in 2025/26 to 9.44% in 2028/29. This indicates sustained pressure on both HRA and General Fund to absorb growing debt service costs within constrained revenues.
findings.matters: Rising financing cost ratios across both funds indicate growing overall debt burden; limits flexibility to invest in service improvements or respond to unexpected pressures

findings.headline: Capital expenditure nearly doubling to £48.9m in 2026/27 with £15.7m prior-year slippage
findings.detail: Planned capital expenditure for 2026/27 is £48,929k, nearly double 2025/26 (£25,306k). Of this, £33,157k is new and £15,772k represents slippage from previous years' programmes. This includes £24,157k General Fund and £24,772k HRA capital spending.
findings.matters: Material prior-year slippage indicates delivery capability concerns; a near-doubling of spend combined with historical underperformance creates risk that the council cannot execute this programme or sustain cash outflows
findings.quote: The below table shows planned expenditure in the 2026/27 Capital Programme of £48,929k, (£33,157k new budget for new or continuing projects plus the projected slippage from prior years of £15,772k).

findings.headline: HRA financing costs escalating to 18.02% of net revenue by 2028/29
findings.detail: The ratio of HRA financing costs (borrowing and long-term obligations) to net revenue stream is forecast to rise from 10.64% in 2025/26 to 18.02% by 2028/29. This means nearly one pound in every five pounds of HRA revenue will be consumed by debt service, driven by the growing HRA capital programme and associated borrowing.
findings.matters: High financing cost ratios indicate growing debt burden consuming revenue that could otherwise fund services; leaves limited room if revenues plateau or costs rise unexpectedly
findings.figures: HRA financing cost ratio: 10.64% (2025/26) rising to 18.02% (2028/29); HRA CFR growing from £56,199k to £83,478k

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 - 2026_27 Capital Strategy and Capital Programme
findings.headline: Pension fund deficit creates future funding obligation
findings.detail: The council has identified a pension fund deficit valued at £9.41m in the latest tri-annual valuation and is committed to making future payments to cover it. This represents an off-balance-sheet liability that will impact future revenue budgets.
findings.matters: Pension liabilities are typically long-term but can accelerate if investment performance deteriorates or if contribution rates are adjusted. This adds to the council's forward revenue commitments alongside capital financing costs.
findings.figures: Pension fund deficit: £9.41m (latest tri-annual valuation)
findings.quote: In addition to the projected debt of £31,233k in 2025/26 detailed in Table 5 above, the Council is committed to making future payments to cover its pension fund deficit (valued at £9.41m within latest pension tri-annual valuation).

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 - 2026_27 Capital Strategy and Capital Programme
findings.headline: Substantial HRA housing development programme with significant council funding dependency
findings.detail: The HRA capital programme includes Project 60 (HRA Development Strategy) budgeted at £32,000k over five years. Though the council hopes to secure grant funding from Affordable Homes Programme and Homes England, the strategy acknowledges 'a substantial element of the cost remains with the Council', requiring new HRA borrowing.
findings.matters: Large borrowing to fund housing development commits future HRA revenue to debt servicing. If rental income does not grow proportionately, or if maintenance backlogs emerge, the HRA could face affordability constraints on routine maintenance.
findings.figures: Project 60: £32,000k over 2026/27–2029/30. HRA Borrowing 50 Yrs for Project 60 and related schemes: £35,138k total over 5 years. HRA planned revenue for housing development: £1,750k (renewable energy) + £11,255k (major repairs reserve).
findings.quote: To fund the proposed Housing Development Schemes, a prudent assumption has been included for the utilisation of 1-4-1 receipts or for additional grant funding to be made available from Homes England and One Public Estate Funding, although a substantial element of the cost remains with the Council.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 - 2026_27 Capital Strategy and Capital Programme
findings.headline: Limited capital receipts reducing financial flexibility for capital funding
findings.detail: The council explicitly forecasts limited capital receipts in 2025/26 onwards due to changes in legislation surrounding Right to Buy. This removes a traditional funding source for capital investment and increases reliance on borrowing or grants.
findings.matters: Capital receipts are a flexible funding source that can be deployed without ongoing revenue impact. Their absence forces greater reliance on debt, which increases annual financing costs and reduces ability to respond to unexpected capital needs.
findings.figures: General Fund capital receipts forecast: 2026/27: £300k; 2027/28 onwards: £0k. HRA capital receipts substantially reduced compared to historical levels.
findings.quote: The Council expects to receive limited Capital Receipts in 2025/26 due to the changes in legislation surrounding the sale of Council Houses through the 'Right to Buy' scheme.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 - 2026_27 Capital Strategy and Capital Programme
findings.headline: Major capital programme dependent on securing external grants that are not yet confirmed
findings.detail: The council's ability to deliver key infrastructure projects—including the Cullompton Relief Road (£26,214k), Waste Depot remodelling, and energy efficiency improvements—relies on securing external grant funding. Section 10.4.1 explicitly states projects will 'only be undertaken if the Council is successful in securing sufficient external funding'. The Waste Depot project was 'initially expected to need to be funded internally' but relies on a recently announced Extended Producer Responsibility grant.
findings.matters: External dependency creates delivery risk and potential for unplanned slippage or reprioritisation. If grants are delayed or not awarded, the council may face pressure to fund these from internal resources, increasing borrowing, or to defer essential infrastructure.
findings.figures: Cullompton Relief Road: £26,214k (HIF funded). Waste Depot remodelling: Extended Producer Responsibility grant funding. Energy efficiency projects: conditional on 'robust business case' and 'securing sufficient external funding'
findings.quote: Projects include 'spend to save' proposals improving the energy efficiency and improving the carbon footprint of our property infrastructure that will only be undertaken if the Council is successful in securing sufficient external funding and is accompanied by a robust business case that demonstrates an acceptable payback.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 - 2026_27 Capital Strategy and Capital Programme
findings.headline: HRA debt trajectory and revenue pressure accelerating significantly
findings.detail: The Housing Revenue Account's Capital Financing Requirement is growing from £56,199k in 2025/26 to £67,627k in 2026/27, then to £83,478k by 2028/29. Financing costs for HRA as a proportion of net revenue stream rise sharply from 10.64% in 2025/26 to 18.02% by 2028/29, nearly doubling in three years.
findings.matters: The HRA operates as a ring-fenced account and cannot be subsidised from general funds. Rapidly rising debt servicing costs constrain the ability to invest in maintenance and new stock, particularly if rental income does not keep pace with borrowing costs.
findings.quote: Housing Revenue Account 16.77% 10.64% 11.57% 15.82% 18.02%

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 - 2026_27 Capital Strategy and Capital Programme
findings.headline: Borrowing requirement increasing sharply with rising revenue implications
findings.detail: The Council's Capital Financing Requirement is forecast to increase by £8,401k in 2026/27, reaching £83,187k by that year. Total debt is projected to rise from £31,233k in 2025/26 to £39,663k in 2026/27. Critically, the proportion of General Fund revenue committed to financing costs (interest and MRP) is rising from 5.69% in 2025/26 to 7.89% in 2026/27, reaching 9.44% by 2028/29.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand the trajectory of debt servicing costs and whether they remain sustainable within available revenue. The rapid increase in both absolute borrowing and its proportion of revenue raises questions about fiscal headroom and sensitivity to interest rate changes.
